summary: The party asks you to run: {recruiter} asks you to run for {open seat}, and what they want back is part of the ask.
realLife: One life: In 1945 a Republican committee in a California district held by the same Democrat looked for a candidate. A banker and family friend wrote to Nixon, then a Navy officer, who flew out, met the committee and won the seat in 1946. Another: In 1922, with his clothing store failing, the Pendergast organization recruited him for county judge, an office that ran county business. He won narrowly and lost in 1924 when a rival faction backed the Republicans. Another: In 1975 Austin Democrats asked her husband David to run for county commissioner. He said no, so they asked her, and she won.
gates: You are a party member or lean to the party.
{open seat} is on the next ballot.
weights: Credentials the party values (service, a law degree, a business).
How far your stances are from the incumbent's.
How many times in a row the party has lost the seat.
choices: ask what they would put behind you, and what it costs once you hold the seat
ask for time to talk it over at home

branches.when: your business or job is failing
branches.then: The ask arrives with the debts on the counter, and the backing comes with a price you name or refuse.
{household member} turns them down and they turn to you. {household member} is stung at being passed over, or relieved, by their traits.
Saying yes means moving home to meet the residency rule, and the talk at home is about the move as much as the race.
Someone else was asked first. A rival brings it up later, and {recruiter} admits it if asked.
A sit-down with the committee follows, and each answer goes on your record as a stance.
